glyph

I built glyph so I could make interactive graphs straight from my R scripts, without writing a lot of extra code just to make a plot interactive. It is for anyone who wants a simpler grammar for interactive graphics in R. glyph is in its early stages, and new features are being added regularly.

install.packages("glyph")

# Development version
# remotes::install_github("josh45-source/glyph")

A first plot 

library(glyph)

glyph(mtcars, x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  mark_point(color = cyl, size = hp) |>
  interact(tooltip = "{cyl} cyl, {mpg} mpg at {wt} tons", zoom = TRUE) |>
  set_scale("y", zero = TRUE, label = "Miles per gallon") |>
  theme_tokens(preset = "dark") |>
  titles(title = "Motor Trend Cars", subtitle = "Weight vs fuel efficiency")

Each step adds to a specification, a plain R list that describes the whole plot. When the plot is printed, glyph compiles the spec to JSON and draws it in the browser with D3.js. That happens at the console and in R Markdown, Quarto and vignettes alike. Call render() only when you want to set the width and height.

What goes in the spec

Marks are the layers that draw data: points, lines, bars, areas, text, rules, ribbons, links and polygons, plus boxplots, violins, sina points and histograms, which summarise a variable’s distribution. Each is a mark_*() function, and mappings are bare column names or expressions such as factor(cyl).

interact() adds tooltips, hover effects, zoom, brushing and click handling. selection() defines named selections, including a clickable legend.

animate() controls how marks enter, and with by = it steps through groups of the data.

compose() puts several plots in one widget and can link their selections. facet(), marginals() and inset() add small multiples, marginal distributions and inset plots.

theme_tokens() sets the look from a few tokens such as font, background and accent. Text and grid colours are derived from the background so they stay readable.

to_vegalite() converts a spec to Vega-Lite JSON, and export() writes a plot to an HTML or JSON file.

Learn more

The Getting Started guide runs through each feature with live plots you can hover, zoom and brush. Using glyph in Shiny shows how to read what the user selects from a Shiny server. The function reference lists everything glyph exports, and ARCHITECTURE.md explains how the spec, the compiler and the renderer fit together.
